metric_rationale: The metric computes the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying heuristic, specifically on the subset of trials where Tallying and Weighted Additive (WADD) make strictly opposite predictions. Under the Tallying model, this proportion will be high (close to 1, subject to noise), whereas under the WADD model, it will be low (close to 0). By isolating the exact trials of disagreement, the metric maximizes the discriminative power between the two theories.

The metric computes the proportion of choices that align with the WADD model's predictions on two maximally dissociative trials (Trial 1 and Trial 3). On these trials, one option has fewer but highly valid features (favored by WADD), while the other option has more but less valid features (favored by Tallying). Because the theories make strictly opposite predictions here, WADD will score highly on this metric, while Tallying will score very poorly, yielding a large and highly significant difference.

In this design, every trial pits a single high-validity feature (Option A) against a larger number of lower-validity features (Option B) such that the sum of the latter exceeds the former. Take The Best (TTB) uses a non-compensatory lexicographic rule, stopping at the first discriminating feature, and thus always chooses Option A. Weighted Additive (WADD) integrates all features, and since Option B has a higher weighted sum, it consistently chooses Option B. The proportion of B choices (mean of the response column) will be near 0 for TTB and near 1 for WADD.

By design, every trial in this experiment pits a single highly-valid feature (favoring Option A) against multiple lower-validity features (favoring Option B). The non-compensatory Take The Best (TTB) model stops at the single best discriminating feature and will invariably choose Option A (response = 0). The compensatory Weighted Additive (WADD) model integrates all features; because the sum of the lower validities exceeds the single highest validity, WADD will predominantly choose Option B (response = 1). Therefore, the overall proportion of choosing Option B (the mean of the `response` column) will be near 0 for TTB (modulo lapse rate) and near 1 for WADD (modulo choice noise), providing a massive and stable quantitative dissociation between the two theories.

In the standard TTB model, the first discriminating feature always determines the choice (subject only to a uniform lapse rate). Since Option A is favored by the highest-validity discriminating feature across all trials in this design, standard TTB predicts the exact same probability of choosing Option B across all trials (P(B) = epsilon / 2), making the difference between any two sets of trials zero. In contrast, Stochastic TTB predicts that search can probabilistically skip features. Thus, trials where Option A is backed by only one early feature (Group 1) will result in a higher probability of eventually reaching features that favor Option B, compared to trials where Option A is backed by two early features (Group 2). The difference in the proportion of Option B choices between these two groups will be near zero for standard TTB and strictly positive for Stochastic TTB.

To overcome the high between-subject variance caused by the uniformly distributed 'p_skip' parameter in Stochastic TTB, this metric binarizes the within-subject difference. Under standard TTB, the difference in Option B choices between trials with many vs. few Option B features is pure noise (driven by epsilon lapses), centered at 0. Thus, a strictly positive difference occurs less than half the time (often exactly 0 when epsilon is low). Under Stochastic TTB, any p_skip > 0 systematically increases Option B choices when more fallback features are available, making the difference reliably positive. Binarizing the effect bounds the metric's variance while preserving a large mean gap between the theories.

This metric calculates the difference in the probability of making the Take-The-Best (TTB) choice between 'Align' trials (where TTB and WADD favor the same option) and 'Conflict' trials (where TTB and WADD favor opposite options). Under the Stochastic TTB (Search Error) model, the probability of choosing the TTB option is largely determined by skipping the first cue, which is identical across these trials; thus, it predicts a very small difference. Under the Strategy Selection model, the WADD component strongly pulls choices away from the TTB option in Conflict trials but reinforces it in Align trials, predicting a large positive difference. By pooling 6 out of 8 trial types, we significantly reduce within-subject variance compared to single-trial comparisons.

By directly comparing trials where Option B has 1 backup feature (Trials 2, 4, 6) against trials where Option B has 3 or 4 backup features (Trials 1, 3, 5), we heavily exploit the WADD component in the Strategy Selection model. Strategy Selection predicts a massive drop in the probability of choosing Option A when B has many backup features because the compensatory WADD strategy strongly flips to favor B. In contrast, Stochastic TTB evaluates sequentially and predicts only a very tiny difference between these trial types, as the choice is still dominantly driven by the first discriminating feature.

By isolating Trial 4 and Trial 6, we find a perfect mathematical tie under the Feature Value Averaging theory. In both trials, Option A and Option B have exactly the same number of positive features (2 and 3, respectively) and exactly the same sum of validities (1.40 and 2.35). As a result, the Averaging model evaluates both options as strictly equal for *any* value of its parameters (gamma, beta, and epsilon), predicting a choice probability of exactly 0.5. By contrast, the Stochastic Take-The-Best theory evaluates features in descending order of validity. In both trials, the highest-validity discriminating feature favors Option A (feature 2), making TTB consistently predict P(A) > 0.5. This metric yields zero parametric variance for the Averaging theory, ensuring a clean and highly significant statistical contrast.

This metric calculates the difference in the probability of choosing Option A between Trial 3 (where Option A has one high-validity feature and two low-validity features) and Trial 1 (where Option A only has the high-validity feature). Under Stochastic Take-The-Best, adding low-validity features to Option A provides 'backups' in case of search errors, so the probability of choosing A should increase or remain high (metric >= 0). Under Feature Value Averaging, adding low-validity features dilutes Option A's overall value, predicting a significant drop in the probability of choosing A (metric < 0).
